questions.question: What is the difference between instance methods, class methods, and static methods in Python?
questions.title: Instance Method vs Class Method vs Static Method
questions.direct_answer: An instance method receives an object as `self`, a class method receives the class as `cls`, and a static method receives neither automatically. Choose according to whether the operation needs instance state, class-level construction or state, or only belongs in the class namespace.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can choose the correct method kind from the state and dispatch the operation needs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `staticmethod` to avoid writing `self` even when the operation needs object state, or hard-coding the class in an alternative constructor.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use an instance calculation, polymorphic class-method factory, and stateless validation in one coherent example.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: An instance method receives the bound object as `self`.
A `@classmethod` receives the actual calling class as `cls`.
A `@staticmethod` receives no implicit object or class argument.
Class methods are well suited to inheritance-friendly alternative constructors.
Static methods are useful only when a class-owned operation needs no class or instance state.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An instance method is the normal method form. Access through an object binds that object as `self`, so the method can read or change per-instance state and can also reach class behaviour through the instance.

A class method is decorated with `@classmethod` and receives the calling class as `cls`. It is useful for operations about the class as a whole, especially alternative constructors. If a subclass calls the factory, constructing `cls(...)` returns the subclass rather than a hard-coded base instance.

A static method is decorated with `@staticmethod` and receives neither `self` nor `cls` automatically. For example, `Temperature.is_valid(value)` can check a rule closely related to the class without needing object state. It behaves much like a namespaced function.

The choice follows required context: use an instance method for one object's data, a class method for the current class or polymorphic construction, and a static method for a class-related utility with no bound context. If the utility is not meaningfully part of the type, a module-level function may be clearer.

sections.title: Binding determines which context arrives automatically
sections.content:
All three forms place a callable under a class attribute, but descriptors change what is returned during access. A normal function binds an instance when accessed through that instance. `classmethod` binds the class, even if access begins from an object. `staticmethod` suppresses automatic binding and returns the wrapped callable without adding a receiver.

The `cls` binding makes factories cooperate with inheritance. `Base.from_text(...)` builds a `Base`, while `Child.from_text(...)` can build a `Child` using the exact same inherited implementation, provided the constructor contract is compatible. Hard-coding `Base(...)` would lose that behaviour.

Static methods communicate ownership rather than access to state. This can keep a small validator beside the type it describes, but too many static methods may signal that ordinary module functions would form a cleaner API. Method kind should reveal dependency, not merely change call syntax.

sections.title: Match the method to the context it needs
sections.content:
| Method kind | Decorator | Implicit first value | Best fit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Instance | None | Current object as `self` | Read or change one object's state |
| Class | `@classmethod` | Calling class as `cls` | Alternative constructors or class-wide behaviour |
| Static | `@staticmethod` | Nothing | Closely related stateless utility |
| Module function | None, outside class | Nothing | Operation not owned by one type |

sections.title: Use all three forms for different responsibilities

questions.question: What is the difference between `isinstance()` and `type()` in Python?
questions.title: isinstance() vs type()
questions.direct_answer: `isinstance(obj, Class)` accepts instances of the class and its subclasses, while `type(obj) is Class` checks for that exact runtime class. Use `isinstance` for most polymorphic type checks and exact `type` comparison only when subclasses must be excluded deliberately.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand subtype-aware checks and how exact checks can break polymorphism.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `type(value) == Parent` and unexpectedly rejecting valid subclass instances.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention tuple checks, ABCs, and preferring capability-based code when no check is needed.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `type(obj)` returns the object's immediate runtime class.
`type(obj) is C` accepts only that exact class.
`isinstance` can check a tuple of accepted types and supports ABC relationships.
Prefer behaviour-based code when an explicit type check is unnecessary.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`type(value)` returns the value's immediate class. Comparing it with `type(value) is Base` is an exact check, so an object of a subclass does not pass even though it inherits the base contract.

`isinstance(value, Base)` is inheritance-aware. It returns true for direct `Base` objects and for objects whose class derives from `Base`. It can also receive a tuple such as `isinstance(value, (str, bytes))`, and it works with abstract-base-class relationships.

For example, if `AdminUser` extends `User`, an authorization helper that accepts all users should use `isinstance(account, User)`. An exact `type(account) is User` would reject the admin and weaken polymorphism. Exact comparison is appropriate only when the distinction itself is required, such as treating the unextended built-in type specially.

Many Python APIs do not need either check. If the code only needs an object to provide `render()`, calling that operation or expressing a `Protocol` can be more flexible than naming concrete types. When a runtime type boundary is genuine, `isinstance` is normally the correct default.

sections.title: Exact identity and subtype membership ask different questions
sections.content:
Every Python value has an immediate class available from `type`. An exact identity comparison asks whether that class object is precisely the one named. It deliberately ignores inherited substitutability, so it is a narrow test.

`isinstance` asks whether the value belongs to a runtime type relationship. Normal subclasses qualify, and ABC machinery can extend the relationship through registration or subclass hooks. This makes the check fit APIs that promise to accept a family rather than one concrete implementation.

Excessive branching on concrete types often signals misplaced behaviour. Polymorphic methods let each object handle its own variation. Runtime checks remain useful at parsing boundaries, validation points, and code where types genuinely represent different data shapes. At those boundaries, choosing an exact or subtype-aware question should be intentional.

sections.title: The result changes for a subclass instance
sections.content:
| Check for an `AdminUser` that inherits `User` | Result | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `type(admin) is AdminUser` | `True` | Exact immediate class matches |
| `type(admin) is User` | `False` | Exact immediate class differs |
| `isinstance(admin, AdminUser)` | `True` | Direct membership |
| `isinstance(admin, User)` | `True` | Subclass relationship is accepted |
| `isinstance(admin, (User, Guest))` | `True` | At least one accepted type matches |

sections.title: See how a subclass changes the two checks
sections.content:
```python
class User:
    pass

class AdminUser(User):
    pass

admin = AdminUser()

print(type(admin) is AdminUser)
print(type(admin) is User)
print(isinstance(admin, AdminUser))
print(isinstance(admin, User))
print(isinstance(admin, (User, str)))
```

The exact base-class comparison is false, while the subtype-aware checks recognize the inherited relationship.
